content.text:
== performs type coercion before comparison.
=== compares without coercion (strict equality).

Senior developers use === almost always to avoid unexpected type coercion bugs.

examples.title: Type Coercion Traps
examples.code:
// ❌ Unexpected coercion with ==
0 == false        // true
"" == false       // true
null == undefined // true
'0' == 0          // true
[] == false       // true

// ✅ Strict equality with ===
0 === false        // false
"" === false       // false
null === undefined // false
'0' === 0          // false
[] === false       // false

content.text:
Use === and !== almost always.

Exception: If you intentionally want 'nullish' check, use value == null to check for both null and undefined.

items: Feature flags that can be false legitimately
Form validation where 0 or empty string are valid values

flashcards.question: Why does 0 == false return true?
flashcards.answer: The == operator performs type coercion. 0 is coerced to boolean false. Use === to avoid this.

examples.title: Wrong: Using !x for Missing Check

items: Form fields where empty string is meaningful
Pagination: page=0 vs missing page parameter

flashcards.question: Why is !value a bad 'missing check' in many systems?
flashcards.answer: Because !value treats 0, empty string, and false as 'missing', which are often valid values. Use value == null instead to check for null/undefined only.

content.text:
undefined often means 'not provided'
null means 'provided and intentionally empty'

This distinction is critical for API contracts and database persistence.

Mixing null and undefined randomly breaks:

• JSON serialization (undefined often disappears)
• API contracts (client vs server misunderstanding)
• DB persistence (null meaning unknown vs empty)

examples.title: PATCH API Pattern

items: PATCH semantics: undefined = don't change, null = clear
JSON APIs (undefined gets stripped, null is preserved)

flashcards.question: What's the difference between null and undefined in API contracts?
flashcards.answer: undefined = 'not provided', null = 'provided and intentionally empty'. In PATCH requests: undefined means don't change, null means clear the value.

examples.title: Weird JavaScript Behaviors
examples.code:
// ❌ typeof pitfalls
typeof null           // 'object' (legacy bug!)
typeof []             // 'object'
typeof function(){}   // 'function'

// ❌ NaN weirdness
NaN === NaN           // false (only value not equal to itself)
typeof NaN            // 'number' (yes, really)

// ❌ Array detection
const arr = []
typeof arr === 'object'  // true (not helpful!)
arr instanceof Array     // true (but fails across iframes)
Array.isArray(arr)       // true ✅ CORRECT WAY

examples.title: Safe Type Checking

items: Preventing 'cannot read property of undefined' crashes

flashcards.question: Why is typeof null === 'object'?
flashcards.answer: It's a legacy bug in JavaScript that can't be fixed without breaking the web. Use x === null to check for null specifically.

flashcards.question: Why does NaN === NaN return false?
flashcards.answer: NaN is the only value in JavaScript not equal to itself. Use Number.isNaN(x) to check for NaN.

examples.title: Number Pitfalls
examples.code:
// ❌ Floating point precision
0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3  // false! (0.30000000000000004)

// ❌ Division by zero
1 / 0              // Infinity (not an error!)
-1 / 0             // -Infinity
0 / 0              // NaN

// ❌ String to number coercion
parseInt('10px')   // 10 (silently ignores 'px')
Number('10px')     // NaN
+'10px'            // NaN

// ❌ NaN comparison
const x = NaN
x === NaN          // false
x == NaN           // false
isNaN(x)           // true (but also true for 'hello')
Number.isNaN(x)    // true ✅ CORRECT

examples.title: Safe Number Handling

items: Scientific calculations (be aware of precision limits)

flashcards.question: Why does 0.1 + 0.2 !== 0.3 in JavaScript?
flashcards.answer: Floating point precision. Binary representation can't exactly represent 0.1 and 0.2. For money, use integer cents or a decimal library.

examples.title: String Comparison Issues
examples.code:
// ❌ Comparing without trimming/normalizing
const input1 = 'abc '
const input2 = 'abc'
input1 === input2  // false

// ❌ Case sensitivity
'Alice' === 'alice'  // false

// ❌ Unicode look-alikes
const a = 'café'  // é as single character
const b = 'café'  // é as e + combining accent
a === b  // might be false!
a.length !== b.length  // different lengths!

examples.title: Safe String Handling

flashcards.question: Why should you normalize strings at API boundaries?
flashcards.answer: To avoid bugs from whitespace, case differences, and Unicode variations. Use trim(), toLowerCase(), and normalize('NFC') for consistent comparison.

content.text:
Domain logic: prefer immutable transformations.
Private local data: mutation is acceptable if it does not escape.
Shared objects: avoid mutation.

This balance prevents bugs while maintaining performance.

examples.title: Mutation Bug
Immutable Transformation

items: Middleware pipelines (each step returns new object)

flashcards.question: When is mutation safe in JavaScript?
flashcards.answer: Mutation is safe for private local data that doesn't escape the function. For shared objects and domain logic, prefer immutable transformations.

content.text:
TypeScript reduces runtime bugs but does not eliminate them.

You still need runtime validation at API boundaries.

TypeScript only validates at compile time - it disappears at runtime.

flashcards.question: Why do you still need runtime validation even with TypeScript?
flashcards.answer: TypeScript only validates at compile time. External data (APIs, DB, user input) can violate type contracts at runtime. Always validate at boundaries.

flashcards.question: What's the difference between compile-time and runtime type safety?
flashcards.answer: Compile-time (TypeScript) catches errors during development. Runtime validation (Zod, Joi) catches errors from external data that TypeScript can't verify.
